issues.legal_issue: The government may appoint multiple government pleaders and assign particular cases to them without giving an existing government pleader exclusive control over all government litigation.
material_facts: An advocate had been authorized to represent the government in civil cases in a district.
During his term, the government appointed additional assistant government pleaders and assigned land acquisition cases to one of them.
The existing government pleader refused to hand over the assigned cases and claimed that he should conduct all the cases himself.
The district had a very large volume of court and tribunal litigation, making the appointment of multiple pleaders conducive to speedy conduct of cases.
issues.conclusion: The government was entitled to appoint multiple government pleaders and assign particular cases to them; the existing pleader had no sole control over the government’s cases.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure defines “Government Pleader” inclusively. Read with Order 27 rules 4 and 8B(c), it permits the government to have as many government pleaders as needed and to place particular cases in the charge of particular pleaders. The provision does not confer exclusive control on one government pleader.

predicates.government_pleader_case_allocation_dispu: The proceeding concerns a government pleader’s challenge to the government’s allocation of its cases.
predicates.existing_pleader_claims_exclusive_contro: An existing government pleader claims the right to conduct all government cases or to control cases assigned to another pleader.
predicates.government_has_multiple_cases: The government has multiple cases requiring representation.

issues.definition: When a government pleader challenges the allocation of government cases while claiming exclusive control and the government has multiple cases, the government may appoint multiple pleaders and assign cases among them.

issues.legal_issue: Administrative guidelines governing government pleaders do not, without more, create an enforceable right to control the allocation of government cases.
material_facts: The government pleader relied on state rules concerning government pleaders and their work.
The court characterized those rules as administrative prescriptions serving as guidelines and found that they did not contradict the government’s power to appoint more than one government pleader.
The dispute concerned the internal allocation of work among government pleaders.
issues.conclusion: The state’s administrative rules did not establish an enforceable right to control the allocation of cases, and the allocation of work was an internal arrangement.
issues.legal_principle: The Bihar rules concerning government pleaders were administrative guidelines, not a source of legal rights. They neither conferred exclusive control over cases nor displaced the government’s authority under section 2(7) of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with Order 27 rules 4 and 8B(c), to appoint multiple pleaders and allocate work.

predicates.government_pleader_case_allocation_dispu: The proceeding concerns a government pleader’s challenge to the government’s allocation of its cases.
predicates.applicable_rules_are_administrative_guid: The rules governing the pleader are administrative prescriptions intended to serve as guidelines.
predicates.rules_do_not_grant_exclusive_control: The applicable rules do not give one government pleader exclusive control over the government’s cases.

issues.definition: When a government pleader challenges case allocation under administrative guidelines that confer no exclusive control, those guidelines create no enforceable right to control the allocation.

issues.legal_issue: The office of a government pleader is a public office.
material_facts: The pleader had been appointed by the government to represent it in civil cases.
The office involved conducting government litigation, and the court recognized that the public is concerned with how such duties are performed.
issues.conclusion: A government pleader holds a public office; the court found no improper political or other impertinent consideration in the conduct challenged in this case.
issues.legal_principle: The court approved the broad view in Ramachandran v. Alagiriswami, A.I.R. 1961 Madras 450, that government pleadership is a public office. The relevant considerations include the source of the office, its tenure, and the duties attached to it. The court cautioned that political or other impertinent considerations in dealing with government law offices may affect the legality of the action and subvert the rule of law.

predicates.state_appointed_counsel: The state appoints a lawyer to serve as its government pleader.
predicates.performs_government_case_duties: The lawyer conducts cases on behalf of the government as part of the office.

issues.definition: When the state appoints a lawyer to conduct government cases as part of the office, the government pleadership is a public office.
